en: The Sutra on the Great Dhāraṇī of the Seven-Crore Buddhamātṛ Cundī, spoken by the Buddha;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was staying in the great city of Yaśovatī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
reflecting and observing out of compassion for all sentient beings of the future,
spoke the Mother-of-Buddhas Cundī Dhāraṇī, including the seven koṭis of past Cundī Tathāgatas and others.
...and so forth, until I now speak it together with you.
He then spoke the Great Mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tadyathā oṃ jvale jvale candre svāhā*. If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās...
If one upholds, maintains, reads,
and recites this dhāraṇī ninety thousand times,
all transgressions committed over immeasurable kalpas, such as the five crimes of immediate retribution, will be extinguished.
All shall be extinguished without remainder.
In whatever place they are born,
they shall all encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
All necessary provisions shall be fully provided according to their wishes.
For immeasurable hundreds of lifetimes, they shall always be able to leave the household life;
if they are lay bodhisattvas, [they shall likewise be so endowed].
By practicing the precepts with firm resolve and without regression,
one will swiftly attain the realization of unsurpassed bodhi and be constantly reborn in the heavens.
They are always loved and respected by the devas,
and are also constantly protected by them.
If they descend to be born among humans, [they are likewise so].
They shall become the sons of imperial houses or be born into noble families;
their households shall be free from calamities and misfortunes.
They will not be afflicted or harmed by the suffering of illness;
they will not fall into the three evil realms of existence;
and whatever they undertake will be successful without fail.
All who hear the teachings he utters will believe and accept them.
One who recites this dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times will behold the śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.
If there are grave offenses such that one cannot see [the deity],
recite [the mantra] another hundred thousand times;
then, within the sacred precinct, black rice will be spat out.
Some see themselves ascending to palaces, or climbing white mountains, or rising into trees;
some see great ponds with swirling waters;
others see themselves soaring through the air with ease.
In some instances, they see celestial maidens speaking wondrous words;
in others, they see themselves within great assemblies listening to the sublime Dharma;
and in yet others, they see themselves plucking out their hair and shaving their heads.
Some eat curd-rice and drink white nectar;
some cross the great ocean or float upon the great river;
some ascend the lion throne or behold the Bodhi tree.
Some see themselves boarding a boat; some see śramaṇas;
some see those wearing white or yellow robes with their heads covered by their garments;
some see the sun and moon; and some see boys and girls.
Alternatively, one may see a milk-tree upon one's own body;
or ascend a tree of flowers and fruit;
or see a black man from whose mouth flames issue forth as he flees away in terror.
Or one may see ill-behaved horses and water buffaloes appearing to fight, retreating and fleeing;
or see oneself eating milk porridge;
or see white flowers with fragrant scents.
If one sees such signs as described above, one should know that the offenses have been extinguished.
However, if there are the grave karmic offenses of the five heinous crimes (ānantarya),
and one is unable to see such signs as described above...
One should further recite it until it reaches one million times;
one will certainly behold signs as previously described.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the merits and the functions performed by this dhāraṇī.
If, before an image of the Buddha,
or before a stūpa, or in a pure place,
one smears the ground with cow dung.
Then, construct a square maṇḍala measuring four cubits on each side.
Furthermore, perform offerings according to the ritual rules using flowers, incense, banners, canopies, food, drink, lamps, and torches,
as far as one's means allow.
If you wish to make a request or aspiration,
you must first perform recitation; then,
empower scented water and scatter it in the eight directions, above, and below to establish the boundary.
Once the boundary has been established,
place a vase of fragrant water in each of the four corners of the maṇḍala and one in its center.
The practitioner, facing east while kneeling on their right knee toward the west,
recites the mantra one thousand and eighty times;
the incense water jar will then spontaneously rotate.
One may move freely in any direction, ascending or descending as one pleases.
Alternatively, one may take a clean earthenware bowl, fumigate it with incense,
and apply fragrant ointments both inside and out.
Fill the vessel with scented water and fine fragrant flowers, place it within the maṇḍala, and perform the recitation according to the previously described method for the flask (*kalaśa*).
In this regard, the bowl (*pātra*) is no different from the flask.
If one wishes to know whether all matters are accomplished or not,
one should burn incense, make a vow, and address the Noble One,
praying: "May you resolve my doubts."
If it turns to the right, know that success is achieved;
if to the left, it is not achieved.
Furthermore, take beautiful flowers and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
He sent a youth to bathe and purify himself, and having him don new, clean garments,
he had him apply powdered incense to his hands and hold flowers to cover his face;
furthermore, with his own hand, [the master] took another flower.
Recite the mantra once and throw [the object] onto the youth's body;
the youth will immediately fall into a stupor and speak of both good and evil.
He will dance and laugh at will, rising, sitting, coming, and going.
Alternatively, upon a clean mirror,
recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over beautiful flowers and scatter them upon the mirror;
the messenger will then appear within the mirror.
Furthermore, using the same method as before, take more fine flowers and scatter them upon the surface of the mirror;
immediately, signs of good and evil will manifest within the mirror itself.
Alternatively, one may use vermilion or fragrant oil.
Anoint the nails of the Great Mother with fragrant oil; having soaked sesame oil in *sumana* flowers, recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Immediately, the forms of devas, monks, bodhisattvas, and buddhas will appear.
If one has doubts regarding matters of the three periods of time,
by inquiring about each one individually, one will know all that is wholesome and unwholesome;
these will then immediately manifest of themselves upon the thumb.
If a person suddenly contracts a malignant illness,
one should take branches of the pomegranate tree, white sacrificial grass (*darbha*), and other such fragrant herbs;
by reciting the mantra while whipping or brushing [the patient] with them, they will immediately be healed.
Alternatively, place kusa grass within clarified butter,
recite the mantra seven times, and cast it into the fire;
burn it so that the smoke may fume over the patient.
It will then be immediately cured.
Alternatively, take a thread spun by a young girl;
recite the mantra once for each knot tied therein.
Having thus completed twenty-one knots,
they should be tied around the necks of small boys or girls who accompany the patient.
All diseases caused by evil spirits, demons, and malevolent influences will be completely cured.
Alternatively, place white mustard seeds in clarified butter and take a small amount of those seeds.
Recite the mantra once and cast [the substance] into the fire each time;
after doing this twenty-one times, the illness will be cured.
Furthermore, smear the ground with *gomaya* (cow dung) and construct a maṇḍala.
Draw his image on the ground with charcoal and lash it with a staff made of pomegranate wood or similar materials;
that ghost will weep and beg to depart.
One should not dare to come again; or else, one may fashion a vajra out of copper, tin, iron, wood, or other materials,
place it beside the patient, and perform recitation.
Even when struck with a staff, it immediately flees.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if someone is possessed by a ghost.
Furthermore, if one is at a distance and unable to come in person,
or if the practitioner is unable to go there themselves,
they should take a willow branch and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
He sent someone to take him away, saying: "Stay! Go!
So-and-so has sent this staff to whip you."
If you do not leave, there is no doubt that you will be harmed.
If you do not leave, they will whip you and then depart.
Furthermore, there is another method.
If one recites this without fail while traveling on the road at night,
there will be no fear or danger from thieves, robbers, tigers, wolves, malevolent spirits, ghosts, or other such perilous places.
By maintaining the mind in recitation and performing the protection of the body, all such obstacles will spontaneously vanish;
or they will give rise to the bodhicitta, or feel fear, or speak words seeking release;
and if one is bound, one will be liberated of one's own accord.
If one wishes to cross rivers, streams, or the great ocean,
and fears the dragons, turtles, and other creatures within the water,
by reciting [the mantra] according to the aforementioned method, one will immediately become free from fear.
If someone is bitten by a snake,
one should immediately have that person circumambulate and recite [the mantra] several times;
they will then be healed.
If one suffers from ailments such as smallpox, carbuncles, scabies, or discharging sores,
take frankincense and mix it with pure earth and water;
recite the mantra twenty-one times over them.
Upon applying it, one is immediately healed.
Furthermore, if the lands suffer from irregularities of flood or drought,
or if epidemics and poisons spread among cattle, horses, and other livestock;
One should place sesame seeds, barley, non-glutinous rice, millet, beans, ghee, honey, curd, fresh milk, wood,
and various other fragrant substances all to one side, burn incense, and make a vow.
To eliminate calamities for all sentient beings,
one should perform the hand-seal (mudrā) and the visualization for protecting the body.
Taking the aforementioned items, one should recite the mantra to empower them.
Cast it into fire and burn it.
Perform this rite three times each day for seven days;
by reciting one thousand and eighty times during each session, one’s wishes will be fulfilled.
It brings peace and happiness to all, and all Three Jewels provide protection and assistance.
It can also fulfill all great vows;
if one wishes to subdue various great ghosts and spirits, they will submit at the mere sight of it.
He took seven grains of the bone-relics and placed them within a white lapis lazuli bowl;
he then took half a sheng of clarified butter and placed that as well into the bowl.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
one should prepare a square maṇḍala measuring one or two cubits with mud before the incense altar and in front of the stūpa.
Place a bowl in the center and take beautiful flowers as an offering.
To the west, set down an incense burner and burn agalloch incense.
Recite the mantra with fervent devotion;
then the śarīra within the bowl shall emit light,
or even produce new śarīra.
At that time, the practitioner took up an incense burner and made a vow while prostrating;
he then immediately went out to collect the śarīra relics and drank the clarified butter (sarpis) entirely.
He placed those śarīra relics in a single bottle of lapis lazuli.
Place it inside a pouch of five-colored silk and wear it upon the head;
then immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas will constantly follow the practitioner,
and all spirits and demons will naturally submit.
When performing the ritual, one shall not eat for one day and one night.
If seeking wealth and abundance,
one should place non-glutinous rice and sesame seeds into ghee and curd with the hands.
Make a small amount of the vow-mantra and recite it seven times,
then cast it into the fire to burn.
Do this according to your capacity for seven days, or up to forty-nine days.
Then, according to their wishes: if one seeks a child,
one should write this dhāraṇī upon birch bark leaves.
Furthermore, paint a youth and wrap it in purple silk;
recite the mantra one thousand and eighty times and place it within your topknot, and you will immediately conceive.
If one wishes to be respected and remembered by others,
one should call the person's name and recite the mantra of their respective family one thousand and eighty times.
She will immediately gain his respect and affection.
If, however, he does not find pleasure in his wife,
one should take a pure vessel, fill it with scented water, and [proceed as follows].
Set it aside in a clean place,
smear a maṇḍala with cow dung,
and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In this manner, perform this rite for all seven vases.
At a pure location, establish a maṇḍala using incense and flowers.
Take the scented water from within the vases to bathe.
If the husband likewise desires her, she may also conceive.
If the wife does not desire the husband, it is also according to the previous method.
If one wishes to subdue [the spirit] Śatru, [one should perform the rite].
Take one *kalpa* [of the herb],
bathe thoroughly with fragrant water,
and take yellow lead mixed with clarified butter.
Smear it over the *kalpa-vṛkṣa* until it is completely covered; then,
having drawn a small maṇḍala, place [the tree] in its center.
Then, arrange five ghee lamps at the four corners and the center,
reciting the aforementioned "Namo."
Recite the mantra one invocation at a time,
consecrating white mustard seeds;
place a single bowl of milk upon the maṇḍala.
He made an offering to this Kāpāla, saying,
"Bring me that Citra."
He was Citra-ratha,
the son of Yama;
he abandoned his chariot and submitted.
Do not allow it to be exhausted; for if it is exhausted, it will obstruct the Path for many kalpas.
If you wish to seek intelligence, take half a *liang* each of stone calamus (*shichangpu*) and ox-gallstone (*niuhuang*).
Grind it into a powder, mix it with clarified butter (*sarpis*), and fashion a maṇḍala before the Buddha.
Recite the mantra five thousand times and consume it;
one will immediately attain intelligence and wisdom.
If one wishes to see all ghosts and spirits,
take ox-gallstone (go-rocanā) and recite the mantra until smoke and fire emerge from it.
If one applies it to the eyes and ingests it as well, one will immediately see.
There is another method:
on the shore of a great ocean, or upon a sandbank in a river, or on a sandy islet.
Using the seal of the stūpa image,
one should stamp it upon the sandy bank;
for each stamp, perform one recitation of the mantra.
One shall form a single stūpa [from the mudrā].
When this has been done sixty thousand times,
one will behold the image of the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Some see the Bodhisattva Tārā or the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
by whom all their heart's desires are fulfilled;
others see them bestowing the wondrous medicines of the immortals and deities.
Some receive the prediction of enlightenment (bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa);
some have questions posed before them;
and according to whatever vows they request, they all attain the stages of a bodhisattva and so forth.
Furthermore, there is another method:
circumambulate an image of the Bodhi tree while practicing walking meditation and reciting the mantra one million times.
He immediately saw Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats preaching the Dharma for him;
desiring to follow a Bodhisattva, he was able to follow him at once,
obtaining whatever he sought according to his wishes.
Eventually, manifesting in this body as a great mantra-seer (vidyādhara),
one immediately attains the ability to travel to the pure lands of the ten directions,
where one serves various Buddhas and hears the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one constantly maintains this dhāraṇī while begging for alms,
one will not be harmed by evil persons, malicious dogs, or similar creatures.
Alms are easy to obtain.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one is before a stūpa, or before an image of the Buddha, or before a śarīra-stūpa.
Recite and maintain this dhāraṇī three hundred thousand times.
Furthermore, from the first day to the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight,
perform a great offering ceremony.
Having fasted for one day and one night,
while reciting with right mindfulness, he beheld the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
who then led that person to his own palace.
Furthermore, there is another dharma:
if a king’s subjects encounter difficulties such as being imprisoned, shackled, or otherwise confined,
by reciting this dhāraṇī, they shall immediately attain liberation.
Furthermore, there is another practice:
if one is before a stūpa for turning the wheel of Dharma,
or before a stūpa at the place of the Buddha’s birth.
Or when the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by means of the jeweled stairs before a stūpa,
or before a śarīra-stūpa—
before such various stūpas as these.
If one performs recitation and circumambulation for a full seven weeks,
one will immediately behold the Bodhisattva Aparājita and the Bodhisattva Hārītī;
all their aspirations will be completely fulfilled.
If they require elixirs of the immortals, he shall immediately bestow them upon them;
furthermore, he shall preach the Dharma for them, pointing out the path to Bodhi.
If there are those who recite this dhāraṇī, [he shall likewise provide for them].
Furthermore, until one sits at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all bodhisattvas serve as one’s supreme friends.
Moreover, this Great Mantra Dhāraṇī of Cundā was spoken by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of the boundless bodhimanda for the benefit of all sentient beings,
if there are sentient beings of meager merit who possess no roots of goodness whatsoever,
and who lack the capacity as a vessel—
For those who lack the factors of enlightenment,
if they hear this Mahāpratisarā Great Dhāraṇī even once or read it once,
the sprouts of the faculties for the factors of enlightenment will immediately arise.
How much more so for those who recite and uphold it without ever flagging or neglecting;
by virtue of these roots of goodness, they will swiftly plant the seeds of Buddhahood and fully accomplish immeasurable merits.
Innumerable sentient beings were distanced from dust and defilement and became definitively established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[The Buddha] then taught the method for the recitation of the Seven-Crore Buddhamātṛ Cundī Dhāraṇī.
Based on the Sanskrit manuscript,
there are one hundred thousand verses;
I shall now briefly explain the sequence of recitation, meditative practice, and offerings.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva,
and seek swift deliverance from birth and death.
First, one must enter the maṇḍala of the samaya-consecration and maintain the prohibitive precepts with firm resolve, without regressing.
Delighting in the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts and practices,
they cultivate the four immeasurables throughout the four modes of conduct and give rise to the four great vows to forever leave the three evil realms behind.
Only when the mind is undistracted during all activities may one enter this secret dharma-gate.
Regarding all methods of recitation and offering:
In whatever location one resides,
one must always bathe for purification and don fresh, clean garments;
one should then adorn the site of practice (maṇḍala) according to what one's means allow.
Regarding the method for the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*),
one must first select a secluded and superior location.
Measure out four cubits each toward the east, west, south, and north.
Construct a square maṇḍala;
dig it to a depth of one cubit,
removing bones, stones, bricks, tiles, poor soil, hair, body down, ash, charcoal, chaff, thorns, insects, ants, and the like.
Fill and level the ground with excellent pure earth.
Take fresh *gomaya* and fine soil,
mix them with fragrant water, and smear them upon the ground.
Whether in a multi-storied pavilion or dwelling on a boat,
one should apply clay according to the ritual rules;
likewise, whether in the mountains or in a fine, clean house.
There is no need to dig the ground;
simply decorate it as before, spread a canopy overhead, and hang banners on all four sides.
If there is an image of the Honored One, the Mother of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, [place it there].
Place [the image] within the maṇḍala,
facing west; if there is no principal deity (iṣṭadevatā), [use a substitute].
One may also obtain [the merit] by making offerings to images of the Buddhas, śarīras, and Mahāyāna sūtras.
One should grind white sandalwood and smear it to create an eight-cornered maṇḍala,
resembling the full moon or an eight-petaled lotus.
Thereupon, using new and pure offering vessels made of gold, silver, refined copper, conch shell, mother-of-pearl, jade, stone, porcelain, wood, and so forth,
one should fill them with various foods and drinks, as well as excellent incense, flowers, lamps, and *argha* water mixed with fragrant perfumes.
Arrange and present offerings according to one's capacity.
If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have previously maintained the practice of the precepts, [one should invite them].
Upon first entering the dharma hall,
one must further repent, make a renewed vow and aspiration, and receive the precepts.
This applies even to a lay bodhisattva.
Upon first entering, one must also personally vow and make aspirations according to one's capacity,
receive the three refuges and the five precepts,
or constantly observe the eight precepts.
If one recites at the three fixed times daily,
then within the ritual enclosure, facing east from the southwest,
one should join the palms with a sincere heart and prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground.
I pay homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
With sincere devotion, I direct my thoughts throughout the entire realm of space;
then, placing my right knee upon the ground, I join my palms with a focused mind.
I, disciple [Name], now before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, openly confess and repent for all the offenses committed by my body, speech, and mind since beginningless time.
I now rejoice in the perfection of merit and wisdom, as well as all various virtues, of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time—
past, present, and future.
Then, assuming either the full lotus posture or the half-lotus posture, settle the mind in meditative equipoise.
Eliminate all discursive thoughts and contemplate how sentient beings within the six realms have been circling through the ocean of birth and death across the six destinies since beginningless time.
"May they all resolve upon bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva,
swiftly attaining liberation.
Thereupon, he rubbed his hands with scented ointment and formed the hand-seal (*mudrā*).
When forming the mudrās, cover your hands with your robe so that others do not see them.
First, bind the Samaya-mudrā of the three families, and then bind the various other mudrās. 1.

The Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family: Regarding the first, the Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family, the characteristics of the mudrā are as follows: the hands of merit and wisdom are both turned upward with palms facing up.
The *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *prajñā*, *upāya*, and *praṇidhāna* fingers are slightly bent and support one another;
the *vīrya* and *bala* fingers press down upon the upper joints of the *praṇidhāna* finger;
the *dhyāna* and *jñāna* fingers are attached to the side of the *vīrya* finger.
It is accomplished immediately.
Recite the sublime mantra: *Oṃ tathāgatavajrāya svāhā*.

Recite this three times and scatter it over the crown of the head with the mudrā. This applies equally to both the Padma-kula and the Vajra-kula. Regarding the second Padma-kula Samaya-mudrā: join the two hands of merit and wisdom together.
The precepts, patience, diligence, skillful means, aspiration,
and power each unfold and slightly bend;
the six pāramitās open like lotus flowers.
Joining the tips of the *tāṇḍava* (thumb) and *prajñā* (forefinger),
and slightly bending them, it is completed.
Recite the wondrous words:
Oṃ padmavajrāya svāhā. Recite this three times. This is the Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family; it is the third mudrā, the Wisdom of the Auspicious Canopy, held with palms facing upward.
When dhyāna, prajñā, dāna, and jñāna intersect, it is accomplished.
Then, recite the wondrous mantra:

Oṃ vajravarāhe svāhā. Recite this three times. (4) The Root Mudrā of the Mother Buddha Cundī. Regarding the fourth root mudrā of the Mother Buddha Cundī, the form of the mudrā is as follows: first, with the two little fingers and the two ring fingers of both hands...
Interlace the fingers so that they enter the palms.
Straighten the two middle fingers upward with their tips touching each other.
Place the tips of the two index fingers against the sides of the upper joints of the two middle fingers.
The second [mudrā] is formed by placing each thumb against the side of its respective index finger.

Recite the root dhāraṇī seven times while reciting the "Wondrous Words. For all subsequent mudrās—whether they are binding, releasing, waving, touching, or sealing—one must likewise disperse them above the crown of the head.
5. The Seal for Expelling All Māras, Evil Ghosts, and Spirits. Fifth: For this seal, first take the middle finger, ring finger, little finger, and thumb of the right hand.
Grasp the three fingers below the middle finger of the left hand.
Next, grasp the nail-edges of those same three fingers of the left hand with the left thumb.
This constitutes the clenched fist.
Join the tips of the two index fingers together, and it is thus accomplished.
The sublime mantra says:
Oṃ kuruḍana hūṃ jaḥ. Recite this once.
Perform three circumambulations of the body clockwise with this mudrā;
doing so constitutes the sixth earth-boundary stake mudrā for binding the earth boundary. As for the form of this mudrā: join the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers of both hands.
Interlace the fingers so that they enter the palms,
with the right hand pressing down upon the left;
bend the left index finger into a hook shape.
The right index finger is held straight upward;
the two thumbs and the two little fingers are brought face-to-face, and thus it is formed.
Miaoyan said:
Recite "Oṃ jñānīkīlaya svāhā" once. With the mudrā, touch the ground with the thumbs three times in the manner of driving a stake;
then cease. 7. The Mudrā for Binding the Boundary of the Wall. This seventh mudrā for binding the boundary of the wall follows the same procedure as the previous mudrā for the stake.
Bend the index finger of the right hand into a hook shape;
the left index finger is then held straight and upright, and the mudrā is thus formed.
The Sublime Speech says:
"Oṃ jvālini-prakāśaya svāhā. Recite this three times and, with the mudrā, sweep it to the right three times; this is the eighth, the Net-Binding Mudrā. This mudrā is the same as the Wall Mudrā.
Open [the hands] and look upward.
Press the tip of the right thumb against the tip of the left index finger;
press the tip of the left thumb against the tip of the right index finger.
The little fingers remain interlocked as before, and it is thus completed.

Miaoyan said: "Oṃ jvalana-jvālā svāhā. Recite this three times, and with the mudrā, wave it toward the sun three times; this constitutes the ninth binding of the Great Boundary of the Outer Fire Court. As for this mudrā: with the left hand, secretly cover the back of the right hand.
The hands are placed one above the other.
Simply extend both thumbs upright,
separated by a distance of about two inches, and it is formed.

The Sublime Speech says: Recite "Oṃ asamañji hūṃ svāhā" three times; with the mudrā, rotate it to the right three times. This is the tenth, the Carriage Mudrā. Regarding the form of this mudrā: first, interlace the two hands inwardly.
Place the right hand over the left,
then open the palms upward.
Extend both index fingers straight, with their tips touching one another.
Using the two thumbs to strike the tips of the two middle fingers,
it is accomplished through their coming and going.
The *Myōgon* says:
Oṃ tulu tulu svāhā. Having bound this mudrā, one should visualize within the celestial palace of Akaniṣṭha, amidst an assembly of Vairocana Tathāgata surrounded by Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
I pray that the Noble One, the Mother Bhagavatī Cundā,
shall mount a chariot adorned with the seven precious jewels;
upon this chariot is a seat of white lotus flowers.
The forms on the seat appear like painted images;
one should contemplate them in the mind as if they were right before one's eyes.
Then, recite the wondrous words three times. (11) This is the eleventh mudrā for summoning and inviting the Noble Ones. It accords with the first root mudrā mentioned previously.
Moving the two thumbs back and forth,
one completes [the mudrā] by summoning three times.
The Wondrous Words say:
Oṃ cile cūle candre hye bhagavati svāhā. Having formed this mudrā, the Noble One descended from the top of Mount Sumeru to the site of practice, where she sat upon a white lotus throne.
Then recite the sublime words three times. (12) Forming the Lotus Seat Mudrā: The twelfth [mudrā], forming the Lotus Seat Mudrā, is performed according to the previous root mudrā;
extend both index fingers toward the body and hold them upright.
It is thus accomplished.
The sublime mantra says: Oṃ kāmala svāhā.

Having formed this mudrā, one should visualize within the maṇḍala a lion throne adorned with various jewels, upon which a white lotus flower has blossomed; there, one installs the Noble One and recites the sublime mantra three times. This is the *argha* (water-offering) mudrā. The thirteenth, the *argha* mudrā, follows the same procedure as the preceding fundamental mudrā.
By using the two thumbs to pinch the side below the first joint at the base of each index finger,
it is formed. Miaoyan said:
Oṃ cile cūle candre amṛte bhagavati pratīccha svāhā. (14) To form the mudrā for bathing: the mudrā for bathing, the fourteenth, is performed as previously described for the *argha* mudrā.
Using the two thumbs, each presses against the side of the middle joint of the two middle fingers; thus it is formed.
Miaoyan said:
Oṃ śānti svāhā. 15. The mudrā for incense: The fifteenth mudrā for incense is the same as the preceding root mudrā;
with the two thumbs...
Pressing the lower joint of the right index finger forms [the mudrā].
The *Myōgon* states:
Oṃ le svāhā. This is the sixteenth *kusumamālā-mudrā* (Flower Garland Mudrā); it conforms to the preceding fundamental mudrā.
Place the two thumbs against the side of the lower joint of the left index finger; this constitutes [the mudrā].
The *Myōgon* states:
Oṃ jūḥ svāhā. The seventeenth mudrā for burning incense: following the previous root mudrā, bend the right index finger and press the tips of the two thumbs together; this completes it.
The Sublime Speech says:
Oṃ le svāhā. This is the mudrā for binding the offerings of food and drink, the eighteenth; it accords with the previous root mudrā.
Using the left index finger,
pinch the tips of the two thumbs, and it is accomplished.
Miaoyan said:
Oṃ juna svāhā. To form the lamp mudrā (the nineteenth):
following the previous root mudrā, use the two index fingers to each grasp the tips of the two thumbs; thus it is formed.
The Sublime Speech says: "Oṃ te svāhā.

Having recited this, each of the mudrās for the scented ointment and so forth should be applied by touching the respective colored objects as an offering. (20) This is the twentieth [mudrā], the Binding of the Arrayed Syllables (*akṣaravyūha-mudrā*). As for the form of this mudrā: with the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers...
Cross the hands inward;
with the two thumbs, the two index fingers,
and the two little fingers all held straight up with their tips touching one another, it is formed.
Having completed this hand-seal,
one should visualize oneself as Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, a body of purple-gold color, and a perfect radiance.
Having visualized this, one touches with the hand-seal:
the syllable Oṃ is placed upon the head,
and the syllable Jña is placed within the eyes.
Following the sequence of each syllable,
one should extend this even to both feet, applying them through ritual touch (*mudrā*).
This explains the method of visualizing the arrangement of the *dhāraṇī* syllables upon the body.
Visualize *Oṃ* placed upon the head, white in color like the moon, emitting immeasurable light that eliminates all obstacles;

this is identical to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Place the syllable *Jaḥ* upon the crown of the person’s head and place [the syllable] on both eyes, its color like the sun and moon, for the purpose of illuminating all who are ignorant.
Place the syllable *ḷe* upon the neck; its color is like deep blue lapis lazuli.
To manifest all colors, visualize the principal syllable at the heart; its color is like pure white, just as the mind is clear and pure.
Place the syllable *ḷe* on both shoulders; its color is yellow like gold. Thus one contemplates these colors.
Visualize the syllable *Cī* in the center; its color is wondrous yellow-white. Quickly cause [the practitioner] to ascend the Path;
visualize the syllable *Ti* on the two thighs; its color is like pale yellow. Quickly realize Bodhi;
visualize the syllable *Svaḥ* on the two shins; its form is reddish-yellow. One should always be able to visualize this.
The syllable HA is placed upon the two feet; its color is like that of the full moon.
The practitioner forms this visualization and thus arranges the syllables while contemplating their colors.
This constitutes the sublime Dharma-gate of Cundī, also known as the true form of the Honored One (Bhagavatī). It can extinguish all sins and bring about auspiciousness.
Like a vajra, a solid mass of firmness—this is called the supreme and eminent dharma of Cundī.
If one constantly practices in this manner, know that such a person will swiftly attain siddhi.
The second root mudrā. The characteristics of this mudrā are as follows: with both hands, interlace the fingers toward the inside.
The two index fingers and the two thumbs are held together, straight and upright; thus it is formed.
The *Myōgon* states:

*Namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnām | Tadyathā | Oṃ jvale jvalini cintye svāhā.* Recite this seven times and apply it to the crown of the head to untie the [knots]. This is the twenty-second mudrā for holding the rosary. Regarding the form of this mudrā: first, take the rosary and place it within the palms of both hands.
Immediately, one should join the palms at the heart,
recite the aforementioned root dhāraṇī three times,
and place the rosary upon the crown of the head.
Then, perform the mudrā for holding the rosary.
Purify the beads. 23.
The Mudrā for Holding the Rosary, the twenty-third: The form of this mudrā is made with the two ring fingers and the two thumbs of both hands.
Place each [hand] over the prayer beads;
with the two hands separated by about one inch,
the remaining fingers slightly spread and bent form [the mudrā].
Recite the mantra for purifying the rosary three times: Oṃ vairocanā-male svāhā.
Having purified the rosary, visualize within your own mind that it is in the mouths of seventy million Buddhamātṛkās.
Seven koṭis of dharanī syllables emerge;
each individual syllable emits five-colored light and enters the mouth of the practitioner.
Rest [the mantra] within the moon disk of one’s own heart;
arrange it clockwise and recite the dhāraṇī of the tutelary deity once.
Then, using the ring finger of the right hand...
Pass one bead through the fingers;
cycle again and again, neither hurried nor slow,
and do not raise your voice.
One must clearly pronounce each syllable so that one hears them oneself.
One should visualize the principal deity and the syllables arrayed upon one's body,
while reciting the mantra and keeping count of the repetitions.
Within a single moment of thought, one must simultaneously observe and see all [the objects];
there must be no omission that causes the mind to become distracted.
This should continue until weariness arises from the practice of contemplation.
Recite according to one's capacity,
whether one thousand, two thousand, or even up to three thousand, four thousand, or five thousand times;
always take a fixed number as the standard.
Even if one has urgent affairs,
the number must not be reduced below one hundred and eight;
this is called "recitation by sound."
If one seeks liberation and wishes to swiftly emerge from birth and death,
one performs this yoga of samādhi through inconceivable and immeasurable contemplative practices.
The practitioner of mindfulness visualizes their own mind as being like a full moon.
It is profoundly serene and pure, with internal and external clearly distinguished.
One should place the syllable Oṃ within the moon in the heart,
followed by the syllables Cche-le, Chu-le, Cundī, and Svāhā.

From the beginning, one should arrange the wheel-rim in a clockwise sequence; observing the meaning of each individual syllable with focused attention and in accordance with the mind, one must not allow them to deviate from one another.
This is called the samādhi of contemplating the arrangement of syllables.
The letter-gateway *Oṃ* signifies the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing within the flow [of phenomena].
Furthermore, it is the most supreme meaning among all dharmas.
The letter-gateway *Cha* signifies the meaning of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) regarding all dharmas.
The syllable-gateway *ḷi* signifies that all phenomena are without marks (*animitta*).
The syllable-gateway *jhu* signifies that all phenomena are without arising or abiding.
The syllable-gateway *ḷi* signifies that all phenomena are without excellence (*anabhirati*).
The gateway of the syllable *ba* signifies that all phenomena are without equal awakening.
The gateway of the syllable *ti* signifies that all phenomena are without grasping or relinquishing.
The gateway of the syllable *sva* signifies that all phenomena are equal and beyond verbal expression.
The gateway of the syllable *ha* signifies that all phenomena are without cause, quiescent, and the meaning of non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Although the meanings of the spoken syllables are established through written characters, they are all ultimately the meaning of being without characters; since there are no characters, [they are thus signless].
One must contemplate each individual meaning and characteristic with thorough attention,
beginning again and again without limit or number, never allowing it to be interrupted.
As for this non-interruption:
It is for the sake of the most excellent meaning of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the flowing stream.
Because of this most excellent meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing,
there is no activity.
It is the meaning of non-action;
therefore, signlessness is the meaning of signlessness.
Therefore, the absence of arising and abiding is the meaning of the absence of arising and abiding.
Therefore, non-enlightenment is the meaning of non-enlightenment;
therefore, non-acceptance and non-rejection is the meaning of non-acceptance and non-rejection.
Therefore, equality is beyond verbal expression.
Because it is the meaning of equality and beyond verbal expression, it is the uncaused, quiescent, and non-abiding nirvāṇa;
because it is the meaning of quiescent and non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is unborn and unceasing, most supreme and uninterrupted,
revolving in an endless cycle;
this is called the recitation of samādhi.
The visualization method for seeking the fulfillment of vows according to Cundī is taught as follows:
if one seeks non-discrimination,
one should visualize non-discrimination and non-recollection.
If one seeks the signless and the formless,
one should contemplate that syllables are without the thought of syllables.
If one seeks the gate of non-duality, [one should contemplate thus].
One should visualize two arms;
if seeking the four immeasurables,
one should visualize four arms.
If one seeks the six supernormal powers,
one should contemplate the six arms;
if one seeks the eightfold noble path, [one should contemplate the eight hands].
One should visualize [the deity] with eight arms.
If one seeks the perfection of the ten pāramitās and the ten bhūmis,
one should visualize [the deity] with ten arms.
If one seeks the Tathāgata’s universally pervasive and vast ground,
one should contemplate the twelve arms;
if one seeks the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), [one should contemplate the eighteen hands].
One should visualize eighteen arms;
this is according to the method for visualizing the painted image.
If one seeks the thirty-two marks, [one should visualize them accordingly].
One should visualize thirty-two arms;
if one seeks the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates,
one should visualize eighty-four arms.
Contemplating in this manner, one shall enter the gate of samādhi of all Tathāgatas—the profound, vast, and inconceivable stage.
This is the foundation of right mindfulness;
this is right suchness; this is right liberation.
Having completed the recitation, visualization, and practice, and wishing to exit the maṇḍala,
one must again follow the previous sequence to form the hand-seals (*mudrā*) for the incense, lamps, food, drink, and so forth.
Having performed the offerings, repentance, and made aspirations as desired,
one should then bind the first root mudrā mentioned previously and recite the root dhāraṇī seven times.
Scatter it upon the crown of the head.
Again, form the previous seal of the chariot,
pointing the two thumbs outward.
Three times, flick the tips of the middle fingers while reciting the sublime mantra:
*Oṃ tulu tulu svāhā*. Recite this three times, then again form the previous mudrā of invitation.
With the two index fingers, open [the gesture] outward three times;
this constitutes sending the Noble One back to his original palace.
The Sublime Words say:
Oṃ cili cili cundé jvale jvale bhagavati svāhā sarvabuddhānāṃ putrāṇām āmantraye svāhā. Recite this three times, and again form the seal of the great boundary for the outer fire-court as before.
Recite the sublime mantra *asamāhita-ni* three times while turning to the left; it is then accomplished.
Furthermore, bind the samaya mudrās of the three families once more.
Recite each of these sublime words once and you will have finished.
Then, exit the maṇḍala as you please and perform walking meditation (caṅkrama) according to your inclination.
Recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Anantamukha*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Nirvāṇa*, or other Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.
One should contemplate, recite,
and explain [the teachings], or use seven *koṭi* of seals of Buddha images and stupas to seal scented clay.
Whether on sand or paper, one may stamp [the mudrā] as much or as little as one desires.
If recited, it possesses merit;
it is as described regarding the meditative states in the sūtras.
Having clearly understood each part in its proper sequence,
one may wish to perform various methods such as *śāntika* (pacification) and so forth, whether for oneself or for others.
Then, proceed with the recitation according to the ritual rules.
This explains the *śāntika* rite;
if one wishes to seek the pacification and elimination of all malevolent spirits, [one should perform this].
Furthermore, those who are intelligent, long-lived,
and seeking liberation should,
within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), face north.
Sit with legs crossed and knees upright.
For clothing, food, drink, incense, flowers, lamps, candles, the ground,
and all such items, use white exclusively.
From the first day of the month until the eighth,
one should perform the rites of recitation and *homa* three times each day.
When performing the recitation, one should first recite the root *dhāraṇī* twenty-one times.
Thereafter, one should recite it starting only from the syllable Oṃ.
The sublime words are:
Oṃ cili cili cinti [name of the person], remove calamities and misfortunes svāhā. This is called the method for performing the pauṣṭika rite.
If one desires to seek increase—
namely, the five supernormal powers, the various treasures of a wheel-turning monarch, the *pūrṇa* vessel, the sword, the auspicious jar, the wish-fulfilling gem,
and the *añjana* ointment— [one should practice].
O Yulika! For those seeking the accomplishment of all treasures such as mirrors, Yue-axes, nooses, tridents, medicinal herbs, and so forth,
one should wear yellow robes, face east, and sit in the full lotus posture.
The incense, flowers, food, drink, fruits, lamps, candles, ground,
and all other offerings used should be yellow in color,
from the eighth day of the month until the fifteenth.
Regarding the practices of recitation, homa, and so forth performed three times daily:
the recitation is as previously described.
The *Suvākyam* states:
Oṃ cili cili cinti, may the requests of such-and-such a person be fulfilled as desired, svāhā. This is the teaching on the *śavaskaraṇa* (summoning) rite.
If one wishes to summon all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, and so forth:
One who is to perform this rite should wear red garments,
face west, and assume the bhadrapīṭha posture.
Incense, flowers, food and drink, fruits, lamps, candles, the ground, and so forth [should be prepared].
Use red [pigments] for both;
from the sixteenth to the twenty-third day,
recite the mantra three times each day.
Regarding the methods for *homa* and so forth, the sublime words are:
*Oṃ cili cili cinti*, [for the purpose of] summoning such-and-such a deity, may my vow be accomplished, *svāhā*. Thus he spoke the *abhicāruka* rite.
If one wishes to subdue all malevolent spirits and ghosts,
as well as those humans and devas who harm the Triple Gem,
or those sentient beings with many karmic offenses and heavy obstacles who are difficult to tame;
Those who wish to give rise to the bodhicitta and cultivate various virtuous deeds should generate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion and perform this rite:
wearing blue robes and facing south, they should sit in a squatting posture with the left foot pressing upon the right.
Use incense and flowers that are not fragrant;
for the ground where fruits are eaten and so forth, use green or black colors.
This continues from the twenty-third day until the end of the month.
Perform the methods of recitation and homa three times daily.
The sublime mantra is:
*HŪṂ CCHĪLE CCHŪLE CANDRE HŪṂ PHAṬ*. Having performed the ritual procedure, one should then recite as usual.
The method for painting the image of the Seven-Crore Buddha-Mother Cundī is explained:
take a pure, uncut piece of white cotton cloth and remove any human hair from it.
The painter observes the eight precepts of the fast.
He does not use glue mixed with pigments;
rather, he prepares the colors in a new bowl and uses them to paint.
The image is of a yellowish-white color,
its body adorned with various ornaments,
and it wears white robes from the waist down.
Upon his robes were floral patterns;
he wore a light, gauzy silk celestial garment with wide sleeves,
secured at the waist with a sash.
The morning glow draped across her body;
her wrists were adorned with bracelets of white conch shells,
and her armlets were embellished with the seven precious jewels.
Each hand wears a finger-ring;
he has eighteen arms and three eyes on his face.
The two upper hands perform the gesture of preaching the Dharma (*dharmacakra-mudrā*).
The second hand on the right bestows fearlessness;
the third hand holds a sword;
and the fourth hand holds a rosary.
In his fifth hand he holds a *bhr̥ṅgāra* fruit—what is called in the Chinese language a "fruit full of seeds"—which does not exist here [in China] but is found in the Western lands.
In his sixth hand he holds an axe (*vāsī*), and in his seventh hand he holds a hook (*aṅkuśa*).
The eighth hand holds a vajra;
the ninth hand holds a jewel garland;
the second left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel banner.
The third hand holds a lotus flower;
the fourth hand holds a water pitcher;
the fifth hand holds a noose.
The sixth hand holds a wheel;
the seventh hand holds a conch;
the eighth hand holds a precious vase.
In the ninth hand, he holds a casket containing the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Below the Bodhisattva is a pond,
in which lotus flowers are placed.
The two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, together support the lotus stalk;
upon the lotus is seated the Bodhisattva Cundī,
her image perfectly circular and adorned with radiant flames.
The image is depicted with a compassionate gaze, looking down at the practitioner who sits below;
holding an incense burner in hand,
the practitioner faces upward toward the Bodhisattva.
Above the Bodhisattva, paint two deities from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
such is the method for the image.
This concludes the *Buddhabhāṣita-saptakoṭi-buddhamātṛcundīdhāraṇīsūtra* along with the methods for recitation and meditative visualization.
